# Superconductors and the Future
## Superconductor applications: Immense promise for the future
Superconductors, which offer no resistance to electrical current and can repel magnetic fields, hold immense promise for future applications.

# Superconductors and the Future
## Superconductor applications: Immense promise for the future
##### Heat from resistance
The electricity that powers many devices, from street lights to sewing machines to laptop computers, nearly always encounters resistance that converts some of its energy to heat. This heat is a major cause of deterioration and breakdown. Expect in a few machines, such as stoves, toasters, and arc furnaces, the heat is unwanted and wastes energy and dollars.
The materials known as superconductors offer no resistance to electrical current — but only at extremely low temperatures. At the same temperatures, superconductors also repel external magnetic fields. Superconductivity was discovered by the Dutch scientist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes in 1911, three years after he liquefied helium. He used the cooling effect of helium’s change from liquid to gas to reach temperatures close to absolute zero — zero degrees Kelvin. The first superconductor was mercury cooled to a temperatures of 4°K.

# Superconductors and the Future
## Superconductor applications: Immense promise for the future
##### Applications
Superconductors already have practical applications, since refrigeration of materials down to the boiling point of liquid helium or hydrogen is feasible, though very expensive. Superconducting materials have been used experimentally to speed up connections between computer chips, and superconducting coils make possible the very powerful electromagnets at work in some of the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machines used by doctors to examine soft tissue inside their patients. In Japan and German, superconducting magnets lift experimental magnetic levitation (maglev) trains above the rails, almost eliminating friction. Some high-energy particle accelerators that physicists use to study atomic structures also use these magnets.
More exciting is the prospect of finding materials in which superconductivity occurs at higher, more usable temperatures. If long-distance power lines could be made of superconducting materials, for example, electric bills would plummet.

# Superconductors and the Future
## Superconductor applications: Immense promise for the future
##### Superconductivity at higher temperatures
Progress in reaching the goal of superconductivity at room temperature has been slow. in 1986 Johann Georg Bednorz and Karl Alex Müller at IBM used a ceramic made of lanthanum, barium, copper, and oxygen (LBCO) to achieve superconductivity at 30°K. A year later Paul Chu of the University of Huston and Maw-Kuen Wu of the University of Alabama substituted yttrium for lanthanum (YBCO) and achieved superconductivity at approximately 90°K. At that temperature, liquid nitrogen, a relatively inexpensive refrigerant, can be used.
LBCO, YBCO, and relatives are the so-called high temperature superconductors that seem to offer much promise for the future.

# Superconductors and the Future
## Superconductor applications: Immense promise for the future
##### Still a mystery
Superconductors have already been put to a number of uses and have enormous potential impact on everyday life. Still, explaining superconductivity has proved difficult. No comprehensive theoretical explanation was offered until 1957, almost fifty years after Onnes’ discovery. And while industry is developing all kinds of practical applications for the latest superconductors, the theory behind them remains a mystery.
"Open data is the only way to move the world forward, learning from give and take to find new ways to connect the dots and have new insights, that is what electrochemistry has done already for hundreds of years."
-Koen Kas, 235th ECS Meeting plenary speaker

Heike Kamerlingh Onnes
Nobel Prize in Physics 1913
Born: 21 September 1853, Groningen, the Netherlands
Died: 21 February 1926, Leiden, the Netherlands
Affiliation at the time of the award: Leiden University, Leiden, the Netherlands
Prize motivation: “for his investigations on the properties of matter at low temperatures which led, inter alia, to the production of liquid helium”
Prize share: 1/1

### Life
Heike Kammerlingh Onnes was born in Groningen, Netherlands, where he also received his doctorate in 1879. He later became a professor at the University of Leiden. There, he set up a modern laboratory where he conducted experiments in low-temperature physics. The same year he received the Nobel Prize for the production of liquid helium, he also discovered the phenomenon of superconductivity—when current passes through a material without any resistance. After World War I, Onnes was active in efforts to reconcile researchers from the Allies and the Central Powers.

### Work
When different substances are cooled to very low temperatures, their properties change. In 1908 Heike Kamerlingh Onnes used an ingenious apparatus to cool helium to liquid form. Fluid helium was carefully studied and also became an important aid for the cooling of different substances and charting their properties at low temperatures. In 1911 Kamerlingh Onnes discovered that the electrical resistance of mercury completely disappeared at temperatures a few degrees above absolute zero. The phenomenon became known as superconductivity.
Six prizes were awarded for achievements that have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind. The 10 laureates' work and discoveries range from optogenetics to efforts to promote peace and international law.

# Superconductors and the Future
## Superconductor applications: Immense promise for the future
Superconductors, which offer no resistance to electrical current and can repel magnetic fields, hold immense promise for future applications.

# Superconductors and the Future
## Superconductor applications: Immense promise for the future
##### Heat from resistance
The electricity that powers many devices, from street lights to sewing machines to laptop computers, nearly always encounters resistance that converts some of its energy to heat. This heat is a major cause of deterioration and breakdown. Expect in a few machines, such as stoves, toasters, and arc furnaces, the heat is unwanted and wastes energy and dollars.
The materials known as superconductors offer no resistance to electrical current — but only at extremely low temperatures. At the same temperatures, superconductors also repel external magnetic fields. Superconductivity was discovered by the Dutch scientist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes in 1911, three years after he liquefied helium. He used the cooling effect of helium’s change from liquid to gas to reach temperatures close to absolute zero — zero degrees Kelvin. The first superconductor was mercury cooled to a temperatures of 4°K.

# Superconductors and the Future
## Superconductor applications: Immense promise for the future
##### Applications
Superconductors already have practical applications, since refrigeration of materials down to the boiling point of liquid helium or hydrogen is feasible, though very expensive. Superconducting materials have been used experimentally to speed up connections between computer chips, and superconducting coils make possible the very powerful electromagnets at work in some of the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machines used by doctors to examine soft tissue inside their patients. In Japan and German, superconducting magnets lift experimental magnetic levitation (maglev) trains above the rails, almost eliminating friction. Some high-energy particle accelerators that physicists use to study atomic structures also use these magnets.
More exciting is the prospect of finding materials in which superconductivity occurs at higher, more usable temperatures. If long-distance power lines could be made of superconducting materials, for example, electric bills would plummet.

# Superconductors and the Future
## Superconductor applications: Immense promise for the future
##### Superconductivity at higher temperatures
Progress in reaching the goal of superconductivity at room temperature has been slow. in 1986 Johann Georg Bednorz and Karl Alex Müller at IBM used a ceramic made of lanthanum, barium, copper, and oxygen (LBCO) to achieve superconductivity at 30°K. A year later Paul Chu of the University of Huston and Maw-Kuen Wu of the University of Alabama substituted yttrium for lanthanum (YBCO) and achieved superconductivity at approximately 90°K. At that temperature, liquid nitrogen, a relatively inexpensive refrigerant, can be used.
LBCO, YBCO, and relatives are the so-called high temperature superconductors that seem to offer much promise for the future.

# Superconductors and the Future
## Superconductor applications: Immense promise for the future
##### Still a mystery
Superconductors have already been put to a number of uses and have enormous potential impact on everyday life. Still, explaining superconductivity has proved difficult. No comprehensive theoretical explanation was offered until 1957, almost fifty years after Onnes’ discovery. And while industry is developing all kinds of practical applications for the latest superconductors, the theory behind them remains a mystery.
"Open data is the only way to move the world forward, learning from give and take to find new ways to connect the dots and have new insights, that is what electrochemistry has done already for hundreds of years."
-Koen Kas, 235th ECS Meeting plenary speaker

## And why a 4-search loop costs about 5 times one search
14 min read
Nov 5, 2026
--
_Originally published in__The AI Engineer__._
Agentic search is a model searching in a loop: it writes a query, reads the results and picks its next move, whether that is another search, a page to open or the answer. For example, a coding agent uses it to find the code behind a bug, and a research agent to gather sources for a report. It costs more than one search, and it often pays off when the first search misses.
> I write The AI Engineer, where every issue ships a tool you can run on your own system. **Get it in The AI Engineer**.

## You Already Run This Loop
You run this loop yourself whenever a first search fails. You type an error message into a search box and skim the results. The page you need is missing, so you rewrite the query from what you just read, open the page that looks closest and answer once you have it. Each step uses what the step before it found.
Hand that loop to a model and you have agentic search. The model writes the query, reads the results and picks the next move. Each call to the model carries only what its request holds, so your code sends the question and every result so far with every call. Re-sending is often where the loop's cost comes from.

## When One Search Gets It Wrong
Real questions often need facts from several pages. The 2022 Self-Ask paper uses the smallest case, 2 facts from 2 pages: who was president of the United States when superconductivity was discovered? In the paper's figure, GPT-3 answered it with no search at all and gave Franklin D. Roosevelt. That answer is wrong, and one search does no better.
The loop splits the question. Its first search asks when superconductivity was discovered and finds 1911. Its second search, written from that answer, asks who was president in 1911 and finds William Howard Taft.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
One search answers from whatever its top result proposes, and the loop writes its second search from what the first one found.
The paper's authors then wrote Bamboogle, 125 questions of this 2-step kind. In the paper's test, Google answered 0.0% of them right from the question as typed. With GPT-3 writing its own follow-up searches, the paper measured 60.0%.
One search is how **RAG** works in its basic form. Retrieval-augmented generation sends the user's words to a search, puts the top results in the prompt and lets the model answer from them. Ask RAG the superconductivity question, and it answers from whatever ranked first. In agentic search, the model can reject those results and search again.
> _🔗 Retrieval by meaning over your own documents is the subject of_**_What is Semantic Search?_**  
>   
>   
> _🔗 Other ways to put a model in the retrieval loop are compared in_**_Agentic RAG vs CUA vs A2A_**

## What Each Part of the Loop Does
When you build a search agent or debug one that answers wrong, you need to know which part does what. To search, the model writes a request such as `search("Brave Search API price")`: the name of a function your code exposes, and its argument. That request is a tool call. Your code runs the function and sends the result back as the next message.
> _🔗 First time handing a model a function to call?_**_What is Function Calling?_**_walks through one call end to end._
Agentic search runs that exchange in a loop, with every decision left to the model: what to search, which page to open and when to answer. The loop has 4 parts:
1.   **The model** writes every query and picks the next move.  
2.   **A search tool** sends the query to a search API, which answers from its index: a stored copy of web pages, organized so a query finds the pages that match it.  
3.   **A fetch tool** downloads one page the model asks to read in full.  
4.   **Your code** starts the run, runs each tool call, sends the result back and stops the run at a cap of 8 model calls.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Your code sends the question and the 2 tools, then runs every tool call and re-sends the whole conversation, until the model answers or your code stops it at 8 calls.
> _🔗 Agents in general?_**_What is an AI Agent?_**_covers the loop in which the model decides when to stop._
You choose who does the searching. Build the search and fetch tools yourself, and your code runs every search, so you see each query and set the cap. Or switch on the search a model provider already offers, and its servers do the searching while you write less code.

## Tools You Use That Already Search in a Loop
You have probably watched this loop without knowing its name. Ask a coding assistant to fix a bug, and it searches your files, reads what it finds and searches again before it answers.
**Coding agents search your code.** Claude Code runs grep and glob, the command-line tools you already use to search file contents and file names, over your repository. Its creator, Boris Cherny, posted in February 2026 that early versions searched a stored index of your files, an approach called RAG. In his words, “we found pretty quickly that agentic search generally works better.” **How Claude Code Actually Works** walks through that search.
**Deep research usually runs the longest loops.** OpenAI’s documentation says its deep research can “find, analyze, and synthesize hundreds of sources”, and that a run “can take tens of minutes”. Anthropic’s own deep research agent is the subject of **How Anthropic Built Multi-Agent Deep Research**.
**Chat assistants search the web, and ChatGPT moved to the loop in 2026.** David Konitzny measured ChatGPT before and after GPT-5.6 became the default in August 2026. A round is one batch of searches the model sends before it reads any results. In his dataset, 94.0% of prompts got a single round before the change. After the change, 43.5% got one round, and the other 56.5% searched again from what the first round found.
> _⚠️_**_Turning on web search can still mean one search._**_OpenAI’s documentation describes non-reasoning web search, in which a model that answers without a thinking step sends your question to the search tool and relays the top results._

## When the Loop Pays Off
A loop that searches again and again can still answer worse than one search. The loop often pays on questions that need more than one page, but only for a model that has learned to run it. The same loop that helps one model can leave another worse off than one search.
BrowseComp-Plus is a 2025 benchmark of hard research questions over a fixed set of documents. Its authors raised gpt-oss-20B’s reasoning effort, the budget it spends thinking before it acts. The extra thinking led it to search 23.87 times per question, up from 1.87. The benchmark scored the model’s right answers at 34.58%, up from 13.37%.
Before you rely on the loop, test it on your own questions. Take 2-step questions whose answers you know and run the loop below twice, once allowing 2 model calls and once allowing 8. Count the right answers each time: if 8 calls do not beat 2, the extra calls are only costing you. That test is a small eval, and **What is an Eval?** shows how to build a bigger one. The Search-R1 paper of March 2025 is the warning. On Qwen2.5–7B, a small open model, loops built by prompting alone scored lower than one search, and only the version trained to run the loop beat it.

## William Taft - Key Events
March 4, 1909
Taft inaugurated
William Howard Taft takes the oath of office, becoming the twenty-seventh President of the United States. Taft had been handpicked by his predecessor, Theodore Roosevelt, and trusted to carry through Theodore Roosevelt's progressivism. Not surprisingly, Taft makes many references to his “distinguished predecessor” in his inaugural address. Nevertheless, a newfound chill had arisen between the two men, mirroring the frigid temperatures in the capital that day.
March 15, 1909
Special session convenes
A special session of the United States Congress convenes to consider revision of the tariff. On March 16, Taft sends a special message to Congress urging prompt revision of the tariff.
April 6, 1909
Peary reaches the North Pole
Robert E. Peary reaches the North Pole.
May 17, 1909
Nellie Taft suffers a stroke
Helen “Nellie” Taft suffers a stroke, leaving her speech impaired. Her recovery lasts approximately one year.
June 16, 1909
Taft's first message to Congress
Delivering a message to Congress, Taft proposes a two-percent tax on the net income of all corporations except banks, which he believes will make up for revenue lost by tariff reductions. He also proposes that Congress adopt a constitutional amendment that would permit the collection of personal federal income taxes.
July 12, 1909
Calling for the Sixteenth Amendment
The Senate passes a resolution calling for a Sixteenth Amendment to the Constitution, authorizing Congress to collect income taxes.
July 15, 1909
Negotiation with China
Taft cables the Chinese regent Prince Chun, requesting that China grant American investors a share of a loan that had been floated in Europe for the purposes of building a railroad in southern China. The Chinese reluctantly grant the United States investment privileges.
August 6, 1909
Payne-Aldrich Tariff Act
Taft signs the Payne-Aldrich Tariff Act, which establishes a Tariff Board and reduces the tariff.
September 14, 1909
Taft tours the South, Southwest
President Taft begins a tour of the southern and western states of the United States.

## William Taft - Key Events
September 17, 1909
Supporting tariffs
While on a tour of the United States, Taft calls the Payne-Aldrich Act “the best” tariff bill ever passed by the Republican Party, leaving both Republican progressives and party regulars dismayed.
October 16, 1909
Taft visits Porfirio DÌaz
Taft visits Mexican dictator Porfirio DÌaz at El Paso, Texas, and at Juarez, Mexico.
November 10, 1909
Taft returns from tour
Taft returns from his trip across the United States, having made 259 speeches. An observer in Winona, MN comments about Taft, “I knew he was good natured but I never dreamed he was so dull.”
November 13, 1909
Charges of conspiracy
Louis Glavis, chief of the Field Division of the Department of the Interior, charges in _Collier's Weekly_ magazine that Secretary of the Interior Richard Ballinger conspired to defraud the public domain in the Alaskan coal fields and that the Taft administration was complicit in Ballinger's wrongdoing.
November 18, 1909
Warships to Nicaragua
Taft orders two U.S. warships to Nicaragua in response to the deaths of 500 revolutionaries, and two of their American advisors, at the hands of Nicaragua dictator José Santos Zelaya. The further threat of American force convinces Zelaya to retire on December 16.
November 20, 1909
Kellog vs Standard Oil
Special government prosecutor Frank Kellogg wins a Court of Appeals case against Standard Oil, which is ruled a monopoly and in violation of the Sherman Anti-Trust Act.
December 20, 1909
General Wood becomes Army Chief of Staff
Taft appoints General Leonard Wood as Chief of Staff of the Army. He also elevates circuit judge Horace H. Lurton to the Supreme Court.
January 7, 1910
Taft fires Gifford Pinchot

## William Taft - Key Events
Taft fires Gifford Pinchot, head of the United States Forest Services, upon the release of a letter Pinchot had written to Senator Dolliver of Iowa on behalf of two of his employees implicated in the _Glavis_ case. Pinchot was a leading conservationist and one of the most recognizable officials in the federal government.
February 1, 1910
Secretary of State tours Central, South America
Secretary of State Philander Knox tours Central and South America on a good-will mission.
March 19, 1910
Republican policy victory
Representative George Norris, a progressive Republican from Nebraska, wins a major procedural victory in the House of Representatives when that body approves a plan by which the members of the House Rules Committee would be elected by the full House, rather than appointed by the Speaker of the House. This represented a major defeat for Speaker “Uncle Joe” Cannon (R-IL), a leading opponent of the progressives.
April 25, 1910
Taft appoints Hughes to the Supreme Court
President Taft appoints Governor Charles E. Hughes of New York to the Supreme Court.
May 20, 1910
Glavis-Ballinger dispute
At a congressional investigation into the Glavis-Ballinger dispute, attorney Louis Brandeis, representing Glavis, reveals damaging information about the Taft administration. Congress clears Ballinger and the Taft administration of any wrongdoing, however.
May 31, 1910
Injunction on freight rates
Taft obtains an injunction to prevent western railroads from raising freight rates. Taft was a fervent anti-trust supporter whose unrelenting anti-trust crusade outmatched even that of Teddy Roosevelt.
June 18, 1910
Taft snubs Roosevelt
Taft elects not to greet Theodore Roosevelt upon the latter's return from Africa, a move that widens the rift between the two men.
June 20, 1910
TR declines Taft's invitation
TR declines Taft's invitation to the White House but praises the President's progress on a number of fronts, including railroad legislation, a postal savings bill, and conservationism.
June 25, 1910
Mann Act

## William Taft - Key Events
Congress passes the Mann Act, also known as the “white slave traffic act,” which prohibits the interstate or international transport of women for “immoral purposes.”
June 25, 1910
Postal Savings Bank Act
Taft signs the Postal Savings Bank Act, which allowed one bank in each state, under federal supervision, to give two percent interest on accounts under $500.
August 31, 1910
Roosevelt's "New Nationalism" speech
TR returns and delivers the most radical speech of his political career at Osawatomie, Kansas. In his “New Nationalism” speech, Roosevelt outlines a new role for the government in dealing with social issues. His program takes American progressivism in a new direction, endorsing conservation, control of trusts, labor protection, and a graduated income tax. It also embraces the growing conviction that the nation must address the plight of children, women, and the underprivileged.
September 5, 1910
Taft rejects joint honor
Taft rejects a proposed dinner, given by the National Conservation Congress, that would honor both himself and TR.
September 7, 1910
The International Court of Arbitration
The International Court of Arbitration at The Hague settles a dispute between Britain and the United States over the Newfoundland fisheries.
September 10, 1910
Regarding Roosevelt
Taft, in a letter to his brother, comments that Roosevelt “has proposed a program ("New Nationalism") which it is absolutely impossible to carry out except by a revision of the federal Constitution. In most of these speeches he has utterly ignored me. His attitude toward me is one that I find difficult to understand and explain.”
September 27, 1910
Taft supports Roosevelt
At the New York State Republican Convention in Saratoga, New York, Taft supports Roosevelt's choice for governor of New York, Henry Stimson.
September 29, 1910
The National Urban League
The National Urban League is formed in New York. Its mission is “to enable African Americans to secure economic self-reliance, parity and power and civil rights.”
November 1, 1910
Taft appoints Willis Van Devanter
Taft appoints Willis Van Devanter to the Supreme Court to replace Justice William Moody.

## William Taft - Key Events
March 4, 1909
Taft inaugurated
William Howard Taft takes the oath of office, becoming the twenty-seventh President of the United States. Taft had been handpicked by his predecessor, Theodore Roosevelt, and trusted to carry through Theodore Roosevelt's progressivism. Not surprisingly, Taft makes many references to his “distinguished predecessor” in his inaugural address. Nevertheless, a newfound chill had arisen between the two men, mirroring the frigid temperatures in the capital that day.

Special session convenes
A special session of the United States Congress convenes to consider revision of the tariff. On March 16, Taft sends a special message to Congress urging prompt revision of the tariff.

Peary reaches the North Pole
Robert E. Peary reaches the North Pole.

Nellie Taft suffers a stroke
Helen “Nellie” Taft suffers a stroke, leaving her speech impaired. Her recovery lasts approximately one year.
June 16, 1909
Taft's first message to Congress
Delivering a message to Congress, Taft proposes a two-percent tax on the net income of all corporations except banks, which he believes will make up for revenue lost by tariff reductions. He also proposes that Congress adopt a constitutional amendment that would permit the collection of personal federal income taxes.

Calling for the Sixteenth Amendment
The Senate passes a resolution calling for a Sixteenth Amendment to the Constitution, authorizing Congress to collect income taxes.

Negotiation with China
Taft cables the Chinese regent Prince Chun, requesting that China grant American investors a share of a loan that had been floated in Europe for the purposes of building a railroad in southern China. The Chinese reluctantly grant the United States investment privileges.

Payne-Aldrich Tariff Act
Taft signs the Payne-Aldrich Tariff Act, which establishes a Tariff Board and reduces the tariff.
September 14, 1909
Taft tours the South, Southwest
President Taft begins a tour of the southern and western states of the United States.

## And why a 4-search loop costs about 5 times one search
14 min read
Nov 5, 2026
--
_Originally published in__The AI Engineer__._
Agentic search is a model searching in a loop: it writes a query, reads the results and picks its next move, whether that is another search, a page to open or the answer. For example, a coding agent uses it to find the code behind a bug, and a research agent to gather sources for a report. It costs more than one search, and it often pays off when the first search misses.
> I write The AI Engineer, where every issue ships a tool you can run on your own system. **Get it in The AI Engineer**.

## You Already Run This Loop
You run this loop yourself whenever a first search fails. You type an error message into a search box and skim the results. The page you need is missing, so you rewrite the query from what you just read, open the page that looks closest and answer once you have it. Each step uses what the step before it found.
Hand that loop to a model and you have agentic search. The model writes the query, reads the results and picks the next move. Each call to the model carries only what its request holds, so your code sends the question and every result so far with every call. Re-sending is often where the loop's cost comes from.

## When One Search Gets It Wrong
Real questions often need facts from several pages. The 2022 Self-Ask paper uses the smallest case, 2 facts from 2 pages: who was president of the United States when superconductivity was discovered? In the paper's figure, GPT-3 answered it with no search at all and gave Franklin D. Roosevelt. That answer is wrong, and one search does no better.
The loop splits the question. Its first search asks when superconductivity was discovered and finds 1911. Its second search, written from that answer, asks who was president in 1911 and finds William Howard Taft.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
One search answers from whatever its top result proposes, and the loop writes its second search from what the first one found.
The paper's authors then wrote Bamboogle, 125 questions of this 2-step kind. In the paper's test, Google answered 0.0% of them right from the question as typed. With GPT-3 writing its own follow-up searches, the paper measured 60.0%.
One search is how **RAG** works in its basic form. Retrieval-augmented generation sends the user's words to a search, puts the top results in the prompt and lets the model answer from them. Ask RAG the superconductivity question, and it answers from whatever ranked first. In agentic search, the model can reject those results and search again.
> _🔗 Retrieval by meaning over your own documents is the subject of_**_What is Semantic Search?_**  
>   
>   
> _🔗 Other ways to put a model in the retrieval loop are compared in_**_Agentic RAG vs CUA vs A2A_**

## What Each Part of the Loop Does
When you build a search agent or debug one that answers wrong, you need to know which part does what. To search, the model writes a request such as `search("Brave Search API price")`: the name of a function your code exposes, and its argument. That request is a tool call. Your code runs the function and sends the result back as the next message.
> _🔗 First time handing a model a function to call?_**_What is Function Calling?_**_walks through one call end to end._
Agentic search runs that exchange in a loop, with every decision left to the model: what to search, which page to open and when to answer. The loop has 4 parts:
1.   **The model** writes every query and picks the next move.  
2.   **A search tool** sends the query to a search API, which answers from its index: a stored copy of web pages, organized so a query finds the pages that match it.  
3.   **A fetch tool** downloads one page the model asks to read in full.  
4.   **Your code** starts the run, runs each tool call, sends the result back and stops the run at a cap of 8 model calls.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Your code sends the question and the 2 tools, then runs every tool call and re-sends the whole conversation, until the model answers or your code stops it at 8 calls.
> _🔗 Agents in general?_**_What is an AI Agent?_**_covers the loop in which the model decides when to stop._
You choose who does the searching. Build the search and fetch tools yourself, and your code runs every search, so you see each query and set the cap. Or switch on the search a model provider already offers, and its servers do the searching while you write less code.

## Tools You Use That Already Search in a Loop
You have probably watched this loop without knowing its name. Ask a coding assistant to fix a bug, and it searches your files, reads what it finds and searches again before it answers.
**Coding agents search your code.** Claude Code runs grep and glob, the command-line tools you already use to search file contents and file names, over your repository. Its creator, Boris Cherny, posted in February 2026 that early versions searched a stored index of your files, an approach called RAG. In his words, “we found pretty quickly that agentic search generally works better.” **How Claude Code Actually Works** walks through that search.
**Deep research usually runs the longest loops.** OpenAI’s documentation says its deep research can “find, analyze, and synthesize hundreds of sources”, and that a run “can take tens of minutes”. Anthropic’s own deep research agent is the subject of **How Anthropic Built Multi-Agent Deep Research**.
**Chat assistants search the web, and ChatGPT moved to the loop in 2026.** David Konitzny measured ChatGPT before and after GPT-5.6 became the default in August 2026. A round is one batch of searches the model sends before it reads any results. In his dataset, 94.0% of prompts got a single round before the change. After the change, 43.5% got one round, and the other 56.5% searched again from what the first round found.
> _⚠️_**_Turning on web search can still mean one search._**_OpenAI’s documentation describes non-reasoning web search, in which a model that answers without a thinking step sends your question to the search tool and relays the top results._

## When the Loop Pays Off
A loop that searches again and again can still answer worse than one search. The loop often pays on questions that need more than one page, but only for a model that has learned to run it. The same loop that helps one model can leave another worse off than one search.
BrowseComp-Plus is a 2025 benchmark of hard research questions over a fixed set of documents. Its authors raised gpt-oss-20B’s reasoning effort, the budget it spends thinking before it acts. The extra thinking led it to search 23.87 times per question, up from 1.87. The benchmark scored the model’s right answers at 34.58%, up from 13.37%.
Before you rely on the loop, test it on your own questions. Take 2-step questions whose answers you know and run the loop below twice, once allowing 2 model calls and once allowing 8. Count the right answers each time: if 8 calls do not beat 2, the extra calls are only costing you. That test is a small eval, and **What is an Eval?** shows how to build a bigger one. The Search-R1 paper of March 2025 is the warning. On Qwen2.5–7B, a small open model, loops built by prompting alone scored lower than one search, and only the version trained to run the loop beat it.

## William Taft - Key Events
March 4, 1909
Taft inaugurated
William Howard Taft takes the oath of office, becoming the twenty-seventh President of the United States. Taft had been handpicked by his predecessor, Theodore Roosevelt, and trusted to carry through Theodore Roosevelt's progressivism. Not surprisingly, Taft makes many references to his “distinguished predecessor” in his inaugural address. Nevertheless, a newfound chill had arisen between the two men, mirroring the frigid temperatures in the capital that day.
March 15, 1909
Special session convenes
A special session of the United States Congress convenes to consider revision of the tariff. On March 16, Taft sends a special message to Congress urging prompt revision of the tariff.
April 6, 1909
Peary reaches the North Pole
Robert E. Peary reaches the North Pole.
May 17, 1909
Nellie Taft suffers a stroke
Helen “Nellie” Taft suffers a stroke, leaving her speech impaired. Her recovery lasts approximately one year.
June 16, 1909
Taft's first message to Congress
Delivering a message to Congress, Taft proposes a two-percent tax on the net income of all corporations except banks, which he believes will make up for revenue lost by tariff reductions. He also proposes that Congress adopt a constitutional amendment that would permit the collection of personal federal income taxes.
July 12, 1909
Calling for the Sixteenth Amendment
The Senate passes a resolution calling for a Sixteenth Amendment to the Constitution, authorizing Congress to collect income taxes.
July 15, 1909
Negotiation with China
Taft cables the Chinese regent Prince Chun, requesting that China grant American investors a share of a loan that had been floated in Europe for the purposes of building a railroad in southern China. The Chinese reluctantly grant the United States investment privileges.
August 6, 1909
Payne-Aldrich Tariff Act
Taft signs the Payne-Aldrich Tariff Act, which establishes a Tariff Board and reduces the tariff.
September 14, 1909
Taft tours the South, Southwest
President Taft begins a tour of the southern and western states of the United States.

## William Taft - Key Events
September 17, 1909
Supporting tariffs
While on a tour of the United States, Taft calls the Payne-Aldrich Act “the best” tariff bill ever passed by the Republican Party, leaving both Republican progressives and party regulars dismayed.
October 16, 1909
Taft visits Porfirio DÌaz
Taft visits Mexican dictator Porfirio DÌaz at El Paso, Texas, and at Juarez, Mexico.
November 10, 1909
Taft returns from tour
Taft returns from his trip across the United States, having made 259 speeches. An observer in Winona, MN comments about Taft, “I knew he was good natured but I never dreamed he was so dull.”
November 13, 1909
Charges of conspiracy
Louis Glavis, chief of the Field Division of the Department of the Interior, charges in _Collier's Weekly_ magazine that Secretary of the Interior Richard Ballinger conspired to defraud the public domain in the Alaskan coal fields and that the Taft administration was complicit in Ballinger's wrongdoing.
November 18, 1909
Warships to Nicaragua
Taft orders two U.S. warships to Nicaragua in response to the deaths of 500 revolutionaries, and two of their American advisors, at the hands of Nicaragua dictator José Santos Zelaya. The further threat of American force convinces Zelaya to retire on December 16.
November 20, 1909
Kellog vs Standard Oil
Special government prosecutor Frank Kellogg wins a Court of Appeals case against Standard Oil, which is ruled a monopoly and in violation of the Sherman Anti-Trust Act.
December 20, 1909
General Wood becomes Army Chief of Staff
Taft appoints General Leonard Wood as Chief of Staff of the Army. He also elevates circuit judge Horace H. Lurton to the Supreme Court.
January 7, 1910
Taft fires Gifford Pinchot

## William Taft - Key Events
Taft fires Gifford Pinchot, head of the United States Forest Services, upon the release of a letter Pinchot had written to Senator Dolliver of Iowa on behalf of two of his employees implicated in the _Glavis_ case. Pinchot was a leading conservationist and one of the most recognizable officials in the federal government.
February 1, 1910
Secretary of State tours Central, South America
Secretary of State Philander Knox tours Central and South America on a good-will mission.
March 19, 1910
Republican policy victory
Representative George Norris, a progressive Republican from Nebraska, wins a major procedural victory in the House of Representatives when that body approves a plan by which the members of the House Rules Committee would be elected by the full House, rather than appointed by the Speaker of the House. This represented a major defeat for Speaker “Uncle Joe” Cannon (R-IL), a leading opponent of the progressives.
April 25, 1910
Taft appoints Hughes to the Supreme Court
President Taft appoints Governor Charles E. Hughes of New York to the Supreme Court.
May 20, 1910
Glavis-Ballinger dispute
At a congressional investigation into the Glavis-Ballinger dispute, attorney Louis Brandeis, representing Glavis, reveals damaging information about the Taft administration. Congress clears Ballinger and the Taft administration of any wrongdoing, however.
May 31, 1910
Injunction on freight rates
Taft obtains an injunction to prevent western railroads from raising freight rates. Taft was a fervent anti-trust supporter whose unrelenting anti-trust crusade outmatched even that of Teddy Roosevelt.
June 18, 1910
Taft snubs Roosevelt
Taft elects not to greet Theodore Roosevelt upon the latter's return from Africa, a move that widens the rift between the two men.
June 20, 1910
TR declines Taft's invitation
TR declines Taft's invitation to the White House but praises the President's progress on a number of fronts, including railroad legislation, a postal savings bill, and conservationism.
June 25, 1910
Mann Act

## William Taft - Key Events
Congress passes the Mann Act, also known as the “white slave traffic act,” which prohibits the interstate or international transport of women for “immoral purposes.”
June 25, 1910
Postal Savings Bank Act
Taft signs the Postal Savings Bank Act, which allowed one bank in each state, under federal supervision, to give two percent interest on accounts under $500.
August 31, 1910
Roosevelt's "New Nationalism" speech
TR returns and delivers the most radical speech of his political career at Osawatomie, Kansas. In his “New Nationalism” speech, Roosevelt outlines a new role for the government in dealing with social issues. His program takes American progressivism in a new direction, endorsing conservation, control of trusts, labor protection, and a graduated income tax. It also embraces the growing conviction that the nation must address the plight of children, women, and the underprivileged.
September 5, 1910
Taft rejects joint honor
Taft rejects a proposed dinner, given by the National Conservation Congress, that would honor both himself and TR.
September 7, 1910
The International Court of Arbitration
The International Court of Arbitration at The Hague settles a dispute between Britain and the United States over the Newfoundland fisheries.
September 10, 1910
Regarding Roosevelt
Taft, in a letter to his brother, comments that Roosevelt “has proposed a program ("New Nationalism") which it is absolutely impossible to carry out except by a revision of the federal Constitution. In most of these speeches he has utterly ignored me. His attitude toward me is one that I find difficult to understand and explain.”
September 27, 1910
Taft supports Roosevelt
At the New York State Republican Convention in Saratoga, New York, Taft supports Roosevelt's choice for governor of New York, Henry Stimson.
September 29, 1910
The National Urban League
The National Urban League is formed in New York. Its mission is “to enable African Americans to secure economic self-reliance, parity and power and civil rights.”
November 1, 1910
Taft appoints Willis Van Devanter
Taft appoints Willis Van Devanter to the Supreme Court to replace Justice William Moody.

Assistant Postmaster General Frank H. Hitchcock resigned from his office in February 1908 to lead the Taft effort.[61] In April, Taft made a speaking tour, traveling as far west as Omaha before being recalled to straighten out a contested election in Panama. He had no serious opposition at the 1908 Republican National Convention in Chicago in June, and gained a first-ballot victory. Yet Taft did not have things his own way: he had hoped his running mate would be a midwestern progressive like Iowa senator Jonathan Dolliver, but instead the convention named Congressman James S. Sherman of New York, a conservative. Taft resigned as Secretary of War on June 30 to devote himself full-time to the campaign.[62][63]
General election campaign
Taft's opponent in the general election was William Jennings Bryan, the Democratic nominee for the third time in four presidential elections. As many of Roosevelt's reforms stemmed from proposals by Bryan, the Democrat argued that he was the true heir to Roosevelt's mantle. Corporate contributions to federal political campaigns had been outlawed by the 1907 Tillman Act, and Bryan proposed that contributions by officers and directors of corporations be similarly banned, or at least disclosed when made. Taft was only willing to see the contributions disclosed after the election, and tried to ensure that officers and directors of corporations litigating with the government were not among his contributors.[64]
1908 Taft/Sherman poster

Taft began the campaign on the wrong foot, fueling the arguments of those who said he was not his own man by traveling to Roosevelt's home at Sagamore Hill for advice on his acceptance speech, saying that he needed "the President's judgment and criticism".[65] Taft supported most of Roosevelt's policies. He argued that labor had a right to organize, but not boycott, and that corporations and the wealthy must also obey the law. Bryan wanted the railroads to be owned by the government, but Taft preferred that they remain in the private sector, with their maximum rates set by the Interstate Commerce Commission, subject to judicial review. Taft attributed blame for the recent recession, the Panic of 1907, to stock speculation and other abuses, and felt some reform of the currency (the U.S. was on the gold standard) was needed to allow flexibility in the government's response to poor economic times, that specific legislation on trusts was needed to supplement the Sherman Antitrust Act, and that the constitution should be amended to allow for an income tax, thus overruling decisions of the Supreme Court striking such a tax down. Roosevelt's expansive use of executive power had been controversial; Taft proposed to continue his policies, but place them on more solid legal underpinnings through the passage of legislation.[66]
Taft upset some progressives by choosing Frank Harris Hitchcock as chairman of the Republican National Committee (RNC), placing him in charge of the presidential campaign. Hitchcock was quick to bring in men closely allied with big business.[67] Taft took an August vacation in Hot Springs, Virginia, where he irritated political advisors by spending more time on golf than strategy. After seeing a newspaper photo of Taft taking a large swing at a golf ball, Roosevelt warned him against candid shots.[68]
1908 electoral vote results
Roosevelt, frustrated by his own relative inaction, showered Taft with advice, fearing that the electorate would not appreciate Taft's qualities, and that Bryan would win. Roosevelt's supporters spread rumors that the president was in effect running Taft's campaign. This annoyed Nellie Taft, who never trusted the Roosevelts.[69] Nevertheless, Roosevelt supported the Republican nominee with such enthusiasm that humorists suggested "TAFT" stood for "Take advice from Theodore".[70]

Bryan urged a system of bank guarantees, so that depositors could be repaid if banks failed, but Taft opposed this, offering a postal savings system instead.[64] The issue of prohibition of alcohol entered the campaign when in mid-September, Carrie Nation called on Taft and demanded to know his views. Taft and Roosevelt had agreed the party platform would take no position on the matter, and Nation left indignant, to allege that Taft was irreligious and against temperance. Taft, at Roosevelt's advice, ignored the issue.[71]
In the end, Taft won by a comfortable margin. Taft defeated Bryan by 321 electoral votes to 162; however, he garnered just 51.6 percent of the popular vote.[72] Nellie Taft said regarding the campaign, "There was nothing to criticize, except his not knowing or caring about the way the game of politics is played."[73] Longtime White House usher Ike Hoover recalled that Taft came often to see Roosevelt during the campaign, but seldom between the election and Inauguration Day, March 4, 1909.[74]
On February 18, 1909, after his election but before his inauguration, Taft was recognized as a Mason at sight at the Scottish Rite Cathedral in Cincinnati.[75]
Presidency (1909–1913)  
Main article: Presidency of William Howard Taft  
Inauguration and appointments  
Further information: Inauguration of William Howard Taft  
1909 inauguration

Taft was sworn in as president on March 4, 1909. Due to a winter storm that coated Washington with ice, Taft was inaugurated within the Senate Chamber rather than outside the Capitol as is customary. The new president stated in his inaugural address that he had been honored to have been "one of the advisers of my distinguished predecessor" and to have had a part "in the reforms he has initiated. I should be untrue to myself, to my promises, and to the declarations of the party platform on which I was elected if I did not make the maintenance and enforcement of those reforms a most important feature of my administration".[76] He pledged to make those reforms long-lasting, ensuring that honest businessmen did not suffer uncertainty through change of policy. He spoke of the need to reduce the 1897 Dingley tariff, of the need for antitrust reform, and for continued advancement of the Philippines toward full self-government.[77] Roosevelt left office with regret that his tenure in the position he enjoyed so much was over and, to keep out of Taft's way, arranged for a year-long hunting trip to Africa.[78]
Soon after the Republican convention, Taft and Roosevelt had discussed which cabinet officers would stay on. Taft kept only Agriculture Secretary James Wilson and Postmaster General George von Lengerke Meyer (who was transferred to the Navy Department). Others appointed to the Taft cabinet included Philander Knox, who had served under McKinley and Roosevelt as Attorney General, as the new Secretary of State, and Franklin MacVeagh as Treasury Secretary.[79][80]
Taft did not enjoy the easy relationship with the press that Roosevelt had, choosing not to offer himself for interviews or photo opportunities as often as his predecessor had.[81] His administration marked a change in style from the charismatic leadership of Roosevelt to Taft's quieter passion for the rule of law.[82]
First Lady's illness
Early in Taft's term, in May 1909, his wife Nellie had a severe stroke that left her paralyzed in one arm and one leg and deprived her of the power of speech. Taft spent several hours each day looking after her and teaching her to speak again, which took a year.[83]

## William Taft
### Overview
William Howard Taft faced the difficult task as President of living up to the legacy of Theodore Roosevelt. Taft so disappointed his predecessor, former mentor, and friend, that Roosevelt opposed his renomination in 1912 and bolted from the Republican Party to form his own "Bull-Moose" party, creating an opening for Democrat Woodrow Wilson in the 1912 presidential election. Taft's lifelong ambition was to serve as Chief Justice of the United States, to which he was appointed after leaving the presidency. He remains the only man in American history to have gained the highest executive and judicial positions.

William Howard Taft was the 27th president of the United States from March 4, 1909, to March 4, 1913. Taft, a Republican from Ohio, and the chosen successor of President Theodore Roosevelt, took office after defeating DemocratWilliam Jennings Bryan in the 1908 presidential election. His presidency ended with his landslide defeat in the 1912 election by Democrat Woodrow Wilson, after one term in office.
Taft sought to lower tariffs—a tax on imports—then a major source of governmental income. However he was out-maneuvered. The new Payne–Aldrich Tariff Act of 1909 raised rates when most people expected reductions. Taft expanded Roosevelt's efforts to break up trusts, launching legal cases against U.S. Steel and other very large companies. Taft made six appointments to the United States Supreme Court, more than all but two other presidents. In foreign affairs, Taft focused on China and Japan, and repeatedly intervened to prop up or remove Latin American governments. ## William Taft
### Overview
William Howard Taft faced the difficult task as President of living up to the legacy of Theodore Roosevelt. Taft so disappointed his predecessor, former mentor, and friend, that Roosevelt opposed his renomination in 1912 and bolted from the Republican Party to form his own "Bull-Moose" party, creating an opening for Democrat Woodrow Wilson in the 1912 presidential election. Taft's lifelong ambition was to serve as Chief Justice of the United States, to which he was appointed after leaving the presidency. He remains the only man in American history to have gained the highest executive and judicial positions.

Roosevelt, frustrated by his own relative inaction, showered Taft with advice, fearing that the electorate would not appreciate Taft's qualities, and that Bryan would win. Roosevelt's supporters spread rumors that the president was in effect running Taft's campaign. This annoyed Nellie Taft, who never trusted the Roosevelts.[69] Nevertheless, Roosevelt supported the Republican nominee with such enthusiasm that humorists suggested "TAFT" stood for "Take advice from Theodore".[70]
texts.17:
Bryan urged a system of bank guarantees, so that depositors could be repaid if banks failed, but Taft opposed this, offering a postal savings system instead.[64] The issue of prohibition of alcohol entered the campaign when in mid-September, Carrie Nation called on Taft and demanded to know his views. Taft and Roosevelt had agreed the party platform would take no position on the matter, and Nation left indignant, to allege that Taft was irreligious and against temperance. Taft, at Roosevelt's advice, ignored the issue.[71]
In the end, Taft won by a comfortable margin. Taft defeated Bryan by 321 electoral votes to 162; however, he garnered just 51.6 percent of the popular vote.[72] Nellie Taft said regarding the campaign, "There was nothing to criticize, except his not knowing or caring about the way the game of politics is played."[73] Longtime White House usher Ike Hoover recalled that Taft came often to see Roosevelt during the campaign, but seldom between the election and Inauguration Day, March 4, 1909.[74]
On February 18, 1909, after his election but before his inauguration, Taft was recognized as a Mason at sight at the Scottish Rite Cathedral in Cincinnati.[75]

Taft was sworn in as president on March 4, 1909. Due to a winter storm that coated Washington with ice, Taft was inaugurated within the Senate Chamber rather than outside the Capitol as is customary. The new president stated in his inaugural address that he had been honored to have been "one of the advisers of my distinguished predecessor" and to have had a part "in the reforms he has initiated. I should be untrue to myself, to my promises, and to the declarations of the party platform on which I was elected if I did not make the maintenance and enforcement of those reforms a most important feature of my administration".[76] He pledged to make those reforms long-lasting, ensuring that honest businessmen did not suffer uncertainty through change of policy. He spoke of the need to reduce the 1897 Dingley tariff, of the need for antitrust reform, and for continued advancement of the Philippines toward full self-government.[77] Roosevelt left office with regret that his tenure in the position he enjoyed so much was over and, to keep out of Taft's way, arranged for a year-long hunting trip to Africa.[78]
Soon after the Republican convention, Taft and Roosevelt had discussed which cabinet officers would stay on. Taft kept only Agriculture Secretary James Wilson and Postmaster General George von Lengerke Meyer (who was transferred to the Navy Department). Others appointed to the Taft cabinet included Philander Knox, who had served under McKinley and Roosevelt as Attorney General, as the new Secretary of State, and Franklin MacVeagh as Treasury Secretary.[79][80]
Taft did not enjoy the easy relationship with the press that Roosevelt had, choosing not to offer himself for interviews or photo opportunities as often as his predecessor had.[81] His administration marked a change in style from the charismatic leadership of Roosevelt to Taft's quieter passion for the rule of law.[82]
First Lady's illness
Early in Taft's term, in May 1909, his wife Nellie had a severe stroke that left her paralyzed in one arm and one leg and deprived her of the power of speech. Taft spent several hours each day looking after her and teaching her to speak again, which took a year.[83]

✦
William Howard Taft served as a Judge, Governor-General of the Philippines, provisional Governor of Cuba, and Secretary of War. As President, Taft proved to be a dedicated "trust-buster," initiating 80 antitrust cases. He supported high Tariffs, modernized the State Department, and reformed the U.S. Postal System. President Taft’s foreign policy focused on so-called "Dollar Diplomacy," which prioritized expanded market access in the Americas and Asia. After losing re-election, he returned to public service as Chief Justice of the United States Supreme Court, becoming the only person in U.S. History to lead both the Executive and Judicial Branches of Government.

William Howard Taft was the 27th president of the United States from March 4, 1909, to March 4, 1913. Taft, a Republican from Ohio, and the chosen successor of President Theodore Roosevelt, took office after defeating DemocratWilliam Jennings Bryan in the 1908 presidential election. His presidency ended with his landslide defeat in the 1912 election by Democrat Woodrow Wilson, after one term in office.
Taft sought to lower tariffs—a tax on imports—then a major source of governmental income. However he was out-maneuvered. The new Payne–Aldrich Tariff Act of 1909 raised rates when most people expected reductions. Taft expanded Roosevelt's efforts to break up trusts, launching legal cases against U.S. Steel and other very large companies. Taft made six appointments to the United States Supreme Court, more than all but two other presidents. In foreign affairs, Taft focused on China and Japan, and repeatedly intervened to prop up or remove Latin American governments. It followed a policy of dollar diplomacy, using American banking investment to bolster influence in Latin America and China, with little success.

His administration was filled with conflict between the conservative wing of the Republican Party, with which Taft often sympathized, and the progressive wing, led by Theodore Roosevelt and Robert M. La Follette. Controversies over conservation and over antitrust cases filed by the Taft administration served to further separate Taft and Roosevelt. Roosevelt challenged Taft at the 1912 Republican National Convention, but Taft was able to use his control of the party machinery to narrowly win his party's nomination. After the convention, Roosevelt left the party, formed the Progressive Party, and ran against Taft and Wilson in the 1912 election. Roosevelt had already blocked LaFollette's ambitions, so he endorsed Wilson. The deep split among Republicans doomed Taft's re-election, giving Democrats control of the White House for the first time in sixteen years, as well as control of Congress. Historians generally consider Taft to have been an average president.
One of a series of candid photographs known as the _Evolution of a Smile_, as Taft learns by telephone from Roosevelt of his nomination for president

After his victory in the 1904 presidential election, Theodore Roosevelt announced that he would not seek re-election in 1908. Roosevelt considered Secretary of War Taft to be his logical successor, although Taft was initially reluctant to run,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_William_Howard_Taft#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson_197337-2) and would have preferred being appointed to the position of chief justice of the Supreme Court.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_William_Howard_Taft#cite_note-WTcampaigns-3) Roosevelt used his control of the party machinery to aid his heir apparent,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_William_Howard_Taft#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson_197337-2) and Roosevelt's political appointees were required to support Taft or remain silent.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_William_Howard_Taft#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPringle_vol_1321%E2%80%93322-4) A number of Republican politicians, such as Treasury SecretaryGeorge Cortelyou, tested the waters for a run, but chose to stay out. New York Governor Charles Evans Hughes ran, but when he made a major policy speech, Roosevelt took steps to minimize coverage of Hughes's candidacy.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_William_Howard_Taft#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPringle_vol_1337%E2%80%93338-5) Taft faced no serious opposition at the 1908 Republican National Convention and he won the presidential nomination on the first ballot. Taft hoped his running mate would be a Midwestern progressive such as Iowa Senator Jonathan Dolliver, but instead the convention named Congressman James S. Sherman of New York, a conservative.

Taft resigned as Secretary of War on June 30 to devote himself full-time to the campaign.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_William_Howard_Taft#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPringle_vol_1348%E2%80%93353-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_William_Howard_Taft#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColetta_197315-7)
1908 Taft/Sherman poster

Taft began the campaign on the wrong foot, fueling the arguments of those who said he was not his own man by traveling to Roosevelt's home at Sagamore Hill for advice on his acceptance speech, saying that he needed "the president's judgment and criticism".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_William_Howard_Taft#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris529-8) He supported most of Roosevelt's policies. Taft argued that labor had a right to organize, but not boycott, and that corporations and the wealthy must also obey the law. He attributed blame for the recent recession, the Panic of 1907, to stock speculation and other abuses, and felt some reform of the currency (the U.S. was on the gold standard) was needed to allow flexibility in the government's response to poor economic times. He also spoke out in favor of revisions to tariff rates and favored strengthening the Sherman Antitrust Act.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_William_Howard_Taft#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColetta_197316%E2%80%9318-9) Taft's opponent in the general election was William Jennings Bryan, the Democratic nominee for the third time in four presidential elections. He campaigned on a progressive platform attacking "government by privilege",[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_William_Howard_Taft#cite_note-10) and portraying Republicans as beholden to powerful corporate interests and to the wealthy.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_William_Howard_Taft#cite_note-11) Given that many of Roosevelt's reforms stemmed from his proposals, the Democrat argued that he himself was the true heir to Roosevelt's mantle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_William_Howard_Taft#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColetta_197315%E2%80%9316-12)

He had no serious opposition at the 1908 Republican National Convention in Chicago in June, and gained a first-ballot victory. Yet Taft did not have things his own way: he had hoped his running mate would be a midwestern progressive like Iowa senator Jonathan Dolliver, but instead the convention named Congressman James S. Sherman of New York, a conservative. Taft resigned as Secretary of War on June 30 to devote himself full-time to the campaign.[62][63]
General election campaign
Taft's opponent in the general election was William Jennings Bryan, the Democratic nominee for the third time in four presidential elections. As many of Roosevelt's reforms stemmed from proposals by Bryan, the Democrat argued that he was the true heir to Roosevelt's mantle. Corporate contributions to federal political campaigns had been outlawed by the 1907 Tillman Act, and Bryan proposed that contributions by officers and directors of corporations be similarly banned, or at least disclosed when made. Taft was only willing to see the contributions disclosed after the election, and tried to ensure that officers and directors of corporations litigating with the government were not among his contributors.[64]
1908 Taft/Sherman poster

Taft began the campaign on the wrong foot, fueling the arguments of those who said he was not his own man by traveling to Roosevelt's home at Sagamore Hill for advice on his acceptance speech, saying that he needed "the President's judgment and criticism".[65] Taft supported most of Roosevelt's policies. He argued that labor had a right to organize, but not boycott, and that corporations and the wealthy must also obey the law. Bryan wanted the railroads to be owned by the government, but Taft preferred that they remain in the private sector, with their maximum rates set by the Interstate Commerce Commission, subject to judicial review. Taft attributed blame for the recent recession, the Panic of 1907, to stock speculation and other abuses, and felt some reform of the currency (the U.S. was on the gold standard) was needed to allow flexibility in the government's response to poor economic times, that specific legislation on trusts was needed to supplement the Sherman Antitrust Act, and that the constitution should be amended to allow for an income tax, thus overruling decisions of the Supreme Court striking such a tax down. Roosevelt's expansive use of executive power had been controversial; Taft proposed to continue his policies, but place them on more solid legal underpinnings through the passage of legislation.[66]
Taft upset some progressives by choosing Frank Harris Hitchcock as chairman of the Republican National Committee (RNC), placing him in charge of the presidential campaign. Hitchcock was quick to bring in men closely allied with big business.[67] Taft took an August vacation in Hot Springs, Virginia, where he irritated political advisors by spending more time on golf than strategy. After seeing a newspaper photo of Taft taking a large swing at a golf ball, Roosevelt warned him against candid shots.[68]
1908 electoral vote results
Roosevelt, frustrated by his own relative inaction, showered Taft with advice, fearing that the electorate would not appreciate Taft's qualities, and that Bryan would win. Roosevelt's supporters spread rumors that the president was in effect running Taft's campaign. This annoyed Nellie Taft, who never trusted the Roosevelts.[69] Nevertheless, Roosevelt supported the Republican nominee with such enthusiasm that humorists suggested "TAFT" stood for "Take advice from Theodore".[70]

Bryan urged a system of bank guarantees, so that depositors could be repaid if banks failed, but Taft opposed this, offering a postal savings system instead.[64] The issue of prohibition of alcohol entered the campaign when in mid-September, Carrie Nation called on Taft and demanded to know his views. Taft and Roosevelt had agreed the party platform would take no position on the matter, and Nation left indignant, to allege that Taft was irreligious and against temperance. Taft, at Roosevelt's advice, ignored the issue.[71]
In the end, Taft won by a comfortable margin. Taft defeated Bryan by 321 electoral votes to 162; however, he garnered just 51.6 percent of the popular vote.[72] Nellie Taft said regarding the campaign, "There was nothing to criticize, except his not knowing or caring about the way the game of politics is played."[73] Longtime White House usher Ike Hoover recalled that Taft came often to see Roosevelt during the campaign, but seldom between the election and Inauguration Day, March 4, 1909.[74]
On February 18, 1909, after his election but before his inauguration, Taft was recognized as a Mason at sight at the Scottish Rite Cathedral in Cincinnati.[75]
Presidency (1909–1913)  
Main article: Presidency of William Howard Taft  
Inauguration and appointments  
Further information: Inauguration of William Howard Taft  
1909 inauguration

Taft was sworn in as president on March 4, 1909. Due to a winter storm that coated Washington with ice, Taft was inaugurated within the Senate Chamber rather than outside the Capitol as is customary. The new president stated in his inaugural address that he had been honored to have been "one of the advisers of my distinguished predecessor" and to have had a part "in the reforms he has initiated. I should be untrue to myself, to my promises, and to the declarations of the party platform on which I was elected if I did not make the maintenance and enforcement of those reforms a most important feature of my administration".[76] He pledged to make those reforms long-lasting, ensuring that honest businessmen did not suffer uncertainty through change of policy. He spoke of the need to reduce the 1897 Dingley tariff, of the need for antitrust reform, and for continued advancement of the Philippines toward full self-government.[77] Roosevelt left office with regret that his tenure in the position he enjoyed so much was over and, to keep out of Taft's way, arranged for a year-long hunting trip to Africa.[78]
Soon after the Republican convention, Taft and Roosevelt had discussed which cabinet officers would stay on. Taft kept only Agriculture Secretary James Wilson and Postmaster General George von Lengerke Meyer (who was transferred to the Navy Department). Others appointed to the Taft cabinet included Philander Knox, who had served under McKinley and Roosevelt as Attorney General, as the new Secretary of State, and Franklin MacVeagh as Treasury Secretary.[79][80]
Taft did not enjoy the easy relationship with the press that Roosevelt had, choosing not to offer himself for interviews or photo opportunities as often as his predecessor had.[81] His administration marked a change in style from the charismatic leadership of Roosevelt to Taft's quieter passion for the rule of law.[82]
First Lady's illness
Early in Taft's term, in May 1909, his wife Nellie had a severe stroke that left her paralyzed in one arm and one leg and deprived her of the power of speech. Taft spent several hours each day looking after her and teaching her to speak again, which took a year.[83]

## William Howard Taft
27th President · 1909–1913
✦
William Howard Taft served as a Judge, Governor-General of the Philippines, provisional Governor of Cuba, and Secretary of War. As President, Taft proved to be a dedicated "trust-buster," initiating 80 antitrust cases. He supported high Tariffs, modernized the State Department, and reformed the U.S. Postal System. President Taft’s foreign policy focused on so-called "Dollar Diplomacy," which prioritized expanded market access in the Americas and Asia. After losing re-election, he returned to public service as Chief Justice of the United States Supreme Court, becoming the only person in U.S. History to lead both the Executive and Judicial Branches of Government.
